title: Reversible solids that store energy at chemical-fuel specific energy

concept.text: The proposed innovation is a rechargeable material-and-cell system that stores and returns electrical energy with specific energy comparable to an explicitly chosen chemical fuel, while retaining useful performance through repeated charging. Specific energy means the energy delivered per unit mass. The defining achievement would combine high specific energy, useful cycle life and complete mass accounting in the same operating cell.

The title's reference to solids identifies the materials-centered challenge: reversible electrode chemistry, stable electrolytes and durable interfaces. It does not require every component to be solid. Relevant approaches include lithium-metal cells with gel or liquid electrolyte components and lithium–air cells that draw oxygen from outside the cell. These architectures must be compared using explicit boundaries for electrodes, electrolyte, packaging, reactants and supporting equipment; removing a material from the cell does not necessarily remove its mass or handling requirements from the operating system.

significance.text: For a fixed electrical-energy requirement, higher whole-cell specific energy directly reduces the mass of storage that must be carried. Combining fuel-comparable specific energy with repeated rechargeability would therefore be a major advance for mass-sensitive electric transport and portable power. Peng and colleagues identify electric aircraft and ships as applications demanding higher specific energy. The revolutionary consequence would be a substantial reduction in the storage-mass constraint, potentially enabling applications whose energy requirements currently impose prohibitive battery mass.

Lithium–air illustrates one route to that benefit. The NIMS account explains that its positive electrode reacts with externally supplied oxygen without the intercalation host used in conventional battery electrodes. Avoiding that host can reduce carried electrode mass. Peng and colleagues separately show why electrolyte, current collectors, separators and packaging also matter: high active-material performance alone does not determine the specific energy of a finished cell.

Conditional synthesis: cell-level fuel comparability would not automatically make a rechargeable power system as portable as a complete fuel-powered system. Fuel heating value measures chemical energy, whereas cell discharge measures delivered electrical energy. A useful comparison must identify the fuel energy basis and account for conversion equipment, containment, oxygen handling and other supporting hardware on the relevant sides. Power delivery, charging time, safety, cost and resource supply could still restrict deployment. A safer cell delivering roughly twice the specific energy of a stated baseline could be an important product advance while remaining below this concept's proposed target.

missing_breakthrough.text: The central unsolved capability in the supplied evidence is simultaneous performance: high electrical energy per kilogram of complete cell, sustained over a service-relevant cycle life at a stated power. NIMS describes a tradeoff in the lithium–air literature it reviews: cells operated at higher cell-level specific energy tend to have shorter cycle lives, while long cycling can be demonstrated under conditions yielding much lower specific energy. This is a documented engineering challenge, not an established law that forbids a better chemistry or architecture.

For lithium-metal cells, reducing electrolyte and other non-active mass makes chemical stability more demanding. Peng and colleagues describe reactions involving common carbonate electrolytes that consume lithium inventory and deplete electrolyte, eventually causing failure. The breakthrough must preserve reversible operation under the lean-electrolyte conditions needed for high specific energy, rather than obtaining stability through quantities of supporting material that erase the mass advantage. Electrode chemistry, electrolyte stability and interfaces must therefore improve together.

A further barrier is translating favorable material-level results into an operating cell. Catalyst-normalized capacity can omit the mass of lithium, electrolyte and other components; reducing current collectors, separators and packaging also has practical limits. A convincing advance must retain its energy advantage after these masses are included. For systems using external reactants, the accounting must additionally make clear whether oxygen or water is supplied from the environment or carried, and which supporting equipment is required.

current_state.text: Peng et al., Nature Communications 16, 11695, published 27 November 2025, report an approximately 11 Ah lithium-metal pouch cell delivering 604.2 Wh/kg including packaging, compared with 626.4 Wh/kg when packaging is excluded. The detailed pouch-cell account reports 560.9 Wh/kg after 100 cycles, corresponding to 92.83% energy retention, at 0.1C charging and 0.2C discharging. The abstract describes operation for more than 100 cycles. These results establish the authors' reported combination of approximately 0.6 kWh/kg and roughly 100 cycles under the stated relatively slow cycling conditions; they do not establish the same performance at higher power. The paper's separate 405-cycle coin-cell result should not be assigned to this pouch-cell demonstration.

The Peng cell uses an in-situ carbonate-based gel electrolyte. The supplement identifies a liquid phase within that gel, so the result should not be described as a ceramic all-solid-electrolyte battery. The paper's introduction places state-of-the-art lithium-ion specific energy around 360 Wh/kg; that is the authors' contextual statement, not an independently established worldwide performance ceiling. The supplied review examined the article text, but did not visually inspect its supporting figures or underlying data. The supplement's extracted representation omitted the contents of multiple tables and image-only figures. Accordingly, the numerical results remain attributed reports rather than independently reproduced measurements.

The Japanese-language NIMS NOW article dated 19 September 2025 attributes 1,000 cycles to Kondori and colleagues under conditions using a capacity of 1,000 mAh per gram of catalyst. NIMS estimates that those conditions correspond to approximately 6.6 Wh/kg at the cell level after considering the mass burden associated with that operating configuration. It separately reports a NIMS lithium–air cell result of 456 Wh/kg for 24 cycles. These figures illustrate why cycle count and specific energy must be evaluated together: the 1,000-cycle account and the 456 Wh/kg result describe different demonstrations.

The 6.6 Wh/kg value is NIMS's calculation, and the 1,000-cycle figure is its account of Kondori's work. The underlying Science paper was not captured for direct inspection in the supplied review. Consequently, the research notes' description of a Li2O chemistry and theoretical gasoline-comparable energy could not be verified against that paper's abstract or methods. Those details remain unconfirmed here, rather than disproved. The saved NIMS text also does not independently establish the complete mass inventory behind its calculation, and the review did not inspect its performance-comparison figure.

Evidence-bounded synthesis: the documented Peng and NIMS results do not demonstrate the proposed combination of fuel-comparable electrical specific energy, complete mass accounting and several hundred useful cycles. They nevertheless represent distinct reported advances and should not be rejected because another supporting claim lacks accessible evidence. The supplied freshness record contains no search entries, so these dated results do not establish the exhaustive worldwide demonstration status as of 1 November 2026 or the later source-retrieval date.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed demonstration: a packaged or fully specified rechargeable cell should deliver electrical specific energy comparable to a numerical chemical-fuel benchmark selected before testing, retain a specified fraction of its delivered energy for at least several hundred cycles, and operate at a stated power. Several hundred cycles is a proposed assessment threshold, not an established consensus standard. The protocol must define the fuel, its energy basis, the numerical meaning of comparable, allowable energy loss, discharge depth and operating conditions. Without those choices, a claim of being in the same order of magnitude is too ambiguous to establish completion.
completion_criteria.label: Proposed demonstration

completion_criteria.text: Proposed accounting protocol: report the masses of electrodes, electrolyte, separators, current collectors and packaging, together with any required carried reactants or supporting equipment. For an air-fed system, distinguish cell-level results from operating-system results and state how oxygen uptake and any required water affect the chosen mass boundary. Publish delivered electrical energy, cycle life and power for the same cell configuration and test conditions. Catalyst-normalized capacity, theoretical reaction energy, a single deep discharge, or a long-life result obtained in a separate low-energy configuration would not satisfy this combined demonstration.
completion_criteria.label: Proposed accounting protocol

completion_criteria.text: Proposed reproducibility and practical-boundary test: an independent group should reproduce the cell-level energy and retention results using sufficiently complete fabrication instructions, component inventories and cycling data. Testing should identify the demonstrated temperature range, charging rate, discharge power and reactant-supply conditions, together with material safety or handling constraints relevant to operation. Success would establish performance within those tested boundaries. It would not by itself establish universal performance across applications, commercial manufacturability or economic competitiveness.
completion_criteria.label: Proposed reproducibility and practical-boundary test

related_concepts.text: Roster-based synthesis: MAS-04, A reliable map from a property specification to a makeable material, could help identify electrode and electrolyte combinations, while MAS-03, General atomically precise covalent construction, could offer ways to construct controlled material architectures. Neither capability alone establishes a rechargeable cell's energy, cycle life or complete mass balance. MAS-07, Programmable growth of load-bearing solids, concerns controlled structural growth rather than reversible energy storage, although fabrication methods could eventually overlap.

Roster-based synthesis: MAS-02, Bulk structural solids that are both near their ideal strength and damage-tolerant, and MAS-09, Structural metals that fully recover from macroscopic fracture in service, concern mechanical performance. Such capabilities could potentially benefit containment or mechanical durability, but strength, damage tolerance and fracture recovery do not demonstrate electrochemical reversibility. MAS-05, Structural solids that remain engineering materials after fusion-level atomic displacement, addresses radiation-induced structural damage; it is a distinct durability problem from preserving a rechargeable cell through cycling.

Roster-based synthesis: MAS-08, An ambient catalytic solid that fixes nitrogen at industrial intensity, shares an interest in material surfaces and chemical reactions under practical conditions. Its defining output is nitrogen fixation at industrial intensity, whereas MAS-06 requires repeated storage and recovery of electrical energy with a favorable complete-cell mass balance. Catalytic activity alone cannot establish the energy-storage target.

Roster-based synthesis: MAS-01, Ambient-pressure room-temperature superconductivity in a manufacturable solid, addresses electrical conduction, while MAS-10, Topologically protected quantum matter outside the dilution refrigerator, addresses robust quantum behavior. Either could have separate relevance to electrical technologies, but neither implies high specific energy or rechargeable storage. MAS-06 remains a distinct materials and electrochemical engineering objective within the roster.

change_log.change: Preserved MAS-06's identity and target while defining solids to allow gel or liquid components and external oxygen.
change_log.reason: The reviewed examples include a gel-electrolyte lithium-metal cell and lithium–air systems; an all-solid interpretation would misrepresent the concept and evidence.

change_log.change: Replaced universal absence and lightest-chemistry assertions with the documented combined energy–life challenge.
change_log.reason: The supplied sources support technical barriers but do not establish an exhaustive worldwide ranking or absence of all qualifying systems.

change_log.change: Expanded the mass boundary to distinguish complete cells, required reactants and operating-system equipment.
change_log.reason: Cell-level specific energy and complete-system portability can differ substantially, especially for externally supplied oxygen.

change_log.change: Reframed the impact as a substantial reduction in storage mass and qualified fuel-equivalent portability.
change_log.reason: Specific energy alone does not eliminate transport constraints or account for power, conversion equipment, safety and deployment economics.

change_log.change: Added Peng's package-included and package-excluded values, cycle-100 energy, cycling rates and the distinction from the separate coin-cell result.
change_log.reason: These details define the scope of the reported achievement and prevent combining results from different cell configurations.

change_log.change: Clarified Peng's gel chemistry and preserved figure, data and supplementary-extraction limitations.
change_log.reason: The reviewed text identifies a liquid phase in the gel, and text extraction does not establish visual inspection or independent reproduction.

change_log.change: Attributed the Kondori cycle count and estimated 6.6 Wh/kg to NIMS, and kept NIMS's 456 Wh/kg for 24 cycles separate.
change_log.reason: The Science paper was unavailable for direct review, and the figures represent different operating conditions and demonstrations.

change_log.change: Qualified the Li2O and theoretical gasoline-comparability details instead of treating them as verified or false.
change_log.reason: Their primary-source support was not captured; that evidence gap does not invalidate the separately supported results.

change_log.change: Removed hydrogen's 39.4 kWh/kg and higher-heating-value attribution from the operative benchmark.
change_log.reason: The referenced HyCon source and a supporting URL were absent. A reproducible criterion instead requires an explicitly selected, substantiated fuel benchmark.

change_log.change: Made cycle count, replication and protocol requirements explicit proposals, and added finite operating boundaries.
change_log.reason: The sources motivate joint energy and cycle-life evaluation but do not establish the proposed thresholds as standards.

change_log.change: Added distinct relationships to every other supplied roster entry and retained a bounded statement of demonstration status.
change_log.reason: Related capabilities must remain separate concepts, and the empty freshness record prevents an exhaustive contemporary status conclusion.

unresolved_issues: The numerical fuel-comparison target remains unspecified, including fuel identity, energy basis and whether the comparison concerns cell electrical output or complete operating systems.
The research notes' hydrogen value of 39.4 kWh/kg and its higher-heating-value attribution cannot be substantiated from the supplied materials because the HyCon source is absent.
Direct verification of the Kondori Science paper, including its Li2O chemistry, theoretical gasoline comparison, methods and full bibliographic details, remains unavailable.
The complete mass inventory and assumptions behind NIMS's approximately 6.6 Wh/kg calculation are not independently established by the supplied review.

Peng's results are reported measurements without independent replication established here; supporting figures and underlying data were not visually inspected, and portions of the supplement were inaccessible in the extracted representation.
No exhaustive worldwide demonstration status as of 1 November 2026 can be determined from the empty freshness record.
The proposed cycle count, retention requirement, discharge depth, power, environmental conditions and treatment of external reactants still require operational specification.
